isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::gate.note: B before E is the intended key (isolate the source first), but E is a mix of scoping (detection & analysis, which the lesson places before containment) and containing the shared drive where encryption is actively spreading; a learner could defensibly put E first. Splitting E into a pure containment action, or making the drive already isolated, would remove the B/E ambiguity.

isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::isc2.cc.d2.note: Statement 7 (recording time-to-detect as a metric) is not explicitly taught; the lesson only says the review asks what worked and what changes. A learner may hesitate between Post-incident and Detection & analysis. Statement 4's word 'blameless' is also untaught but harmless.

isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::isc2.cc.d2.answer: The four phases are preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity. You contain first because isolating the compromised system stops the attack spreading and stops the attacker steering it, while eradication takes time and an active attacker could undo it or reinfect clean systems. You keep the machine powered on because memory holds running processes and live connections, evidence that is lost when power is cut. A playbook is a written plan for one kind of incident, such as ransomware or a compromised mailbox, with concrete steps and named owners. The final phase, the lessons-learned review, feeds back into preparation, so the plan and playbooks improve for the next incident.
isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::isc2.cc.d2.note: Lesson justifies 'contain first' mainly by stopping spread; 'eradicate before recover' is its sharper ordering argument. Prompt asks why contain before eradicate, which the lesson covers only implicitly.

isc2.cc.d3.least-privilege::isc2.cc.d3.l.note: Statement 6 (run the monthly payroll report) is not part of the stated job ('processes salary changes that a manager has approved'), so a strict least-privilege reader could answer Remove it. Either add report-running to the job description or replace the statement. Statement 1 is well taught via separation of duties.

isc2.cc.d3.least-privilege::isc2.cc.d3.l.answer: Least privilege means every account, whether a person, service or script, gets only the minimum access its job needs. Need-to-know applies the same idea to information: even someone cleared for a type of data sees only the records their work requires. Blast radius is what an attacker can reach once an account is compromised; it equals whatever that account could reach, so tight scoping limits the damage. Privilege creep is access piling up as people change roles and keep old rights; regular access reviews remove what is no longer needed. The right to delete audit logs is especially dangerous because it lets someone erase the record of what they did, breaking separation of duties and hiding an attack.

isc2.cc.d4.subnetting::gate.note: Lesson's mask list (128..252 for 1..6 bits) gives 192 for /26 directly; well taught by the worked example.

isc2.cc.d4.subnetting::isc2.cc.d4.subnet.answer: Subtract the prefix from 32 to get the host bits; for /25 to /30 the split falls in the last octet. Find the mask value in that octet (128, 192, 224, 240, 248 or 252) and subtract it from 256 to get the block size. Subnets start at multiples of the block size. The network address is the multiple at or just below the host's last octet; the broadcast address is the next multiple minus one. Usable hosts are 2 to the power of the host bits, minus 2. Check that broadcast minus network equals block size minus one. Two addresses are unusable because the all-zeros host address identifies the network itself and the all-ones address is the broadcast for every host.

isc2.cc.d5.security-awareness::gate.note: Every phishing line both comes from a non-yourcompany.com domain and asks for a credential/money, and every legitimate line does neither, so either cue alone sorts the set; consider one legitimate message from an outside domain (a real supplier) or one internal-looking sender with an odd request to force combining cues. Statement 8 (subdomain calendar.yourcompany.com) and 4 (yourcompany.com as a prefix of a foreign domain) are the good discriminating cases; subdomain reading is only implicitly taught.

isc2.cc.d5.security-awareness::isc2.cc.d.answer: Phishing uses email, vishing uses phone calls, and pretexting uses an invented story that makes a request seem normal; tailgating and business email compromise are others. They rely on urgency, authority, secrecy and requests that skip the normal process. To check a suspicious message, look first at who really sent it, the actual address rather than the display name; then at what it wants, such as a credential, money or an opened file; then whether that request would normally arrive this way. If in doubt, verify through a channel you already know and report it. For passwords, current NIST guidance favours long passphrases, a unique password per site kept in a password manager, MFA everywhere, and changes only after suspected exposure.

isc2.cc.d5.logging-monitoring::gate.note: 07:38:41 to 07:38:49 = 8 s; accounts root, admin, test. Note the pattern (three accounts, a few tries each) is guessing-like rather than spraying, consistent with the alert; no success from that source.

isc2.cc.d5.logging-monitoring::isc2.cc.d.answer: Worth logging are authentication events, successful and failed, with their source; privilege changes such as new accounts or admin-group additions; configuration changes like firewall rules or installed software; access to sensitive data; and security tools' alerts. A SIEM collects logs from across the organisation, normalises them into one format, correlates events from different sources and raises alerts when a rule matches. Synchronised clocks let events be put in order across systems, and logs shipped to a separate protected store cannot be erased by an intruder with admin rights. For a suspected brute-force attack, establish where the attempts came from, how many there were, which accounts were tried, over what time span, and whether any attempt from that source succeeded.

isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::hint0.note: Gives a reusable test (reversibility while the attacker is active) that orders eradicate before recover; does not echo any step wording. Distinct from hint1.

isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::hint1.note: 'Without destroying what you will later need to understand it' maps directly onto step B's 'but leave it powered on', singling B out as first; it also quietly resolves the B/E ambiguity by design rather than by understanding. Not a duplicate of hint0 (first step vs. dependency ordering).

isc2.cc.d3.least-privilege::hint0.note: Blast-radius framing; a method, no option wording echoed. Distinct from hint1 (threat lens vs. job-derived lens), though both lead to the same filtering.

isc2.cc.d3.least-privilege::hint1.note: Deriving verbs from the job description (monitor, triage, document, escalate) before reading options is a sound method; the prompt's own verbs line up closely with A/E/H/I, but that is the prompt, not the hint.

isc2.cc.d4.subnetting::hint0.note: Restates the block-size method from the lesson but focuses a stuck learner on the last octet; method only.

isc2.cc.d4.subnetting::hint1.note: Repeats the lesson's 'check yourself' step almost verbatim in spirit; useful as a check but does not help a learner who cannot find the block. Not a duplicate of hint0 (find vs. verify).

isc2.cc.d5.security-awareness::hint0.note: 'All the way to the end' specifically unlocks statement 4 (yourcompany.com.mailbox-support.io); still a method, and the sender-domain cue alone sorts the whole gate, so this hint nearly solves it. Distinct from hint1.

isc2.cc.d5.security-awareness::hint1.note: Channel-mismatch test from the lesson; echoes 'portal you normally use' / 'usual ticket portal' phrasing in statements 5 and 6 slightly, but as a principle, not a shortcut.

isc2.cc.d5.logging-monitoring::hint0.note: Prevents the common error of counting the two 'Accepted' analyst lines; method only.

isc2.cc.d5.logging-monitoring::hint1.note: Mostly obvious from the blank label 'Seconds from the first to the last failed attempt'; adds little. Not a duplicate of hint0, but weak; a hint about checking for a success from the same source, or counting distinct accounts, would do more.
